What this page practises

Warm-up

Say it the exam way

Stellar objects emit radiation over a of wavelengths. A hotter object has a peak wavelength. At every wavelength, it emits energy per unit area per second.

So a red star is than a blue star. The cosmic microwave background radiation is evidence for the theory. So is the dark night sky, known as paradox.

Answers

Say it the exam way

(1) wide range · (2) shorter · (3) more · (4) cooler · (5) Big Bang · (6) Olbers'

2024 Paper 1, Question 9: answer D

  • A Not this one. I is correct, but III is too: star Y's curve is above star X's, so Y emits more energy per second per unit area.
  • B Not this one. II is wrong. Star W is the coolest. Its peak is at the longest wavelength, so the lowest frequency.
  • C Not this one. III is correct, but I is too: star Z's curve is highest and peaks at the shortest wavelength, so Z is the hottest.
  • D Right. I: Z's curve is highest and peaks at the shortest wavelength, so Z is hotter than W. III: Y's curve is above X's. II is wrong: W is coolest, so its peak frequency is the lowest.
  • E Not this one. II is wrong. Star W is the coolest, so its peak is at the longest wavelength and the lowest frequency.

Specimen Paper 1, Question 11: answer D

  • A Not this one. The photoelectric effect is about light releasing electrons from a metal. These two observations are about the whole Universe.
  • B Not this one. The Bohr model explains line spectra from atoms. These two observations are about how the Universe began.
  • C Not this one. Special relativity is about time dilation and length contraction. These observations are about how the Universe began.
  • D Right. The cosmic microwave background is radiation left over from the hot early Universe. Olbers' paradox, the dark night sky, means the Universe has not been there for ever. Both support the Big Bang.
  • E Not this one. Newton's law is about the gravitational force between masses. These observations are evidence about how the Universe began.

2017 Section 1, Question 7: answer D

  • A Not this one. I is correct, but III is correct too: at every frequency, a hotter object emits more.
  • B Not this one. III is correct, but I is too: stellar objects emit over a wide range of frequencies.
  • C Not this one. II is wrong. Hotter objects have a shorter peak wavelength, not a longer one.
  • D Right. I and III are correct. II is wrong: hotter objects have a shorter peak wavelength.
  • E Not this one. II is wrong: hotter objects peak at a shorter wavelength.

2016 Section 1, Question 7: answer C

  • A Not this one. Star Q's curve is higher and peaks at a shorter wavelength, so Q is the hotter star. I is wrong.
  • B Not this one. Star Q's curve is higher at every wavelength, so Q emits more radiation per unit surface area, not P.
  • C Right. Q's curve peaks further left, at a shorter wavelength. I and II are wrong: Q's curve is higher everywhere, so Q is hotter and emits more.
  • D Not this one. Both I and II are wrong. Q's curve is higher and peaks at a shorter wavelength, so Q is hotter and emits more.
  • E Not this one. III is right, but II is wrong. Q's curve is higher, so Q emits more per unit surface area.
